# 118 · Hold route variable renamed in the template but not in the parameter: a 500 on every request of it

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: 7 boundary changes** | functional | high | refactor, behaviour change not intended | [`HoldController`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/ticketing-service/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/ticketing/api/HoldController.java) | [B12: Boundary contracts](../../lib/README.md) |

> The developer renames the path variable of `GET /holds/{id}` to `{holdId}`, so the route reads like the OpenAPI description, and leaves the handler's parameter as `@PathVariable String id`. Spring binds a `@PathVariable` by name, the annotation's or the parameter's, at request time: no template of the route has a variable named `id`, so every request of the route ends in `MissingPathVariableException`, a 500. The code compiles, the context starts, and the module's unit tests, which call the service and not the route, pass. The boundary contract now checks each handler's request binding; the regenerated contract has a `!` line under the renamed route: `@PathVariable id matches no variable in /holds/{holdId}`.

Tags: [spring-boot](../README.md#tag-spring-boot), [request-binding](../README.md#tag-request-binding), [contract-diff-review](../README.md#tag-contract-diff-review)

## The change

Rename the variable in the route template of `HoldController.get` from `{id}` to `{holdId}`, with a comment saying the order and concert routes will follow, and leave the parameter `@PathVariable String id` as it was. The path the client calls does not change.

**Before** ([`HoldController.java`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/ticketing-service/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/ticketing/api/HoldController.java), line 14):

```java
    this.holds = holds;
}

@GetMapping("/holds/{id}")
ConcertController.Hold get(@PathVariable String id) {
    return ConcertController.Hold.of(holds.get(id));
}
```

**After:**

```java
    this.holds = holds;
}

/** The variable is named for what it is, as in the OpenAPI description; the order and concert routes follow. */
@GetMapping("/holds/{holdId}")
ConcertController.Hold get(@PathVariable String id) {
    return ConcertController.Hold.of(holds.get(id));
}
```

A line is a route, listener, schedule, bean definition or configuration key, the advice on a member, a property of a wire type, or a `!` line where an annotation does not do what it says; a member's line changes with its signature and parameter annotations.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`:ticketing-service:test`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

`@PathVariable` with no name of its own takes the parameter's name, `id`, and looks for a variable of that name among the matched route's template variables. After the change the template has `holdId` and nothing else, so `RequestMappingHandlerAdapter` cannot resolve the argument and throws `MissingPathVariableException`, which `DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver` turns into a 500 (a developer error, not a client one, so not a 400 or 404): every `GET /holds/{holdId}` fails, the client that follows the `Location` of a `201` from `POST /concerts/{id}/holds` gets an error for a hold that exists, and the system test of the hold path, which needs Docker and a Kafka, is the first thing that notices. Nothing before that does: the rename compiles (the template is a string), the context starts (the mapping is valid), the controller's parameter is the same, and the unit tests go through `HoldService`. A reviewer reading the diff sees a one-line rename in a string and a comment that makes it sound deliberate.

## Why the verdict is right

The boundary contract renders each handler with its routes and its parameters (`GET /holds/{id} => Hold get(@PathVariable String id)`) and now checks that each parameter can bind to the request: a `@PathVariable` binds by its annotation's name or, failing that, the parameter's, and that name has to be a variable of every template of the route. The developer sees a rename, so the runner regenerates the contract and the reviewer reads the diff: the route line changes from `GET /holds/{id}` to `GET /holds/{holdId}`, which a reviewer might wave through as the rename it is, and under it a new line, `! @PathVariable id matches no variable in /holds/{holdId}: MissingPathVariableException, a 500 on every request`. The `!` line is the violation.

## What to do

Rename the parameter too (`@PathVariable String holdId`), or name the variable in the annotation (`@PathVariable("holdId") String id`), which is the form that survives the next rename of either side. Either way the `!` line goes and the diff under `HoldController` is the renamed route alone, which is what the reviewer approves. The comment promising the same for the order and concert routes is a reason to do them in the same change, with the contract diff showing all three routes renamed and no `!` line under any.

## Notes

- The first example of the request binding checks (`lib/src/binding.rs`), which read a handler's parameter annotations against its routes and its bytecode. A `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam`, `@RequestHeader`, `@CookieValue` or `@MatrixVariable` binds by name: the annotation's `value` or `name`, else the parameter's name as the `MethodParameters` attribute records it (what `javac -parameters` writes and what Spring reads by reflection; the `LocalVariableTable` of `-g`, which Spring 6.0 fell back to, is not read by 6.1). Four things are `!` lines: a `@PathVariable` whose name is a variable of no template of the route (this example; `{id:\\d+}` and `{*rest}` count as `id` and `rest`, and a `Map` parameter takes every variable and needs no name); a named binder on a parameter whose name is not in the bytecode, which fails every request with a 500 (compile with `-parameters`, as the Spring Boot Gradle and Maven plugins do by default and Box Office's conventions do by hand, or name it in the annotation); a `required = false` binder with no `defaultValue` on a primitive, which cannot be null when the request leaves it out (a 500 instead of the 400 a missing required parameter gets); and two `@RequestBody` parameters, the second of which always reads an empty body.
- Two handlers on one route are found across the module: the same route rendered identically on two methods (`GET /tasks/open` twice) is a duplicate Spring refuses at startup (`IllegalStateException: Ambiguous mapping`), reported under both; the same pattern under different variable names (`/tasks/{id}/owner` and `/tasks/{key}/owner`) registers twice, since the patterns differ as strings, and every request that matches both finds them equally specific, so Spring throws `Ambiguous handler methods` for it, a 500. The pattern key drops the variable names and the constraints inside the braces; `consumes`, `produces`, `params` and `headers` stay in the key, so two routes that differ in them are not reported (Spring tells them apart by the request's headers). The Box Office contracts regenerated unchanged: every `@PathVariable` of the three modules names a variable of its route, the modules compile with `-parameters`, and no two handlers share a pattern.
- What the checks do not know: a mapping annotation of the application's own composed of `@RequestMapping` (its elements are not read as paths), a `@PathVariable` on a `@ModelAttribute` or an `@InitBinder` method, a route whose template comes from a constant in another class (the string is in the annotation either way, so this one is fine), a parameter name available to Spring through a `ParameterNameDiscoverer` of the application's own, and the HEAD and OPTIONS requests Spring answers for a GET route. The `required = false` check reads `required` and `defaultValue` as written on the annotation, and `Optional<T>` is an object, not a primitive, so it passes.
- The runner compiles the module with Gradle, reads the runtime class path through the build's `printRuntimeClasspath` task, and runs `jvmcontract update` then `verify` with `--resources` and `--classpath`; the module's Spring Boot tests need Docker for Testcontainers, and are recorded as the tests' result. By hand, `./gradlew :ticketing-service:verifyBoundaries --rerun` with the patch applied reports the route added under its new template with the `!` line and `reads HoldDocument` under it, the old route removed, and `1 problems` in the module's statistics.

**Provenance:** Constructed from the way Spring binds path variables (`MissingPathVariableException` is a 500, raised at request time, when no template variable has the parameter's name) and from the Spring Boot 3.2 upgrade notes, where the end of `LocalVariableTable` parameter name discovery made every unnamed `@PathVariable` and `@RequestParam` of a module built without `-parameters` fail the same way; the Box Office hold route is the one whose template a developer would rename first, since it is the only route whose variable is not under a class-level prefix that names the resource.
